entries.93968754c2c730c068ce6b2a36aeba9b0cd8e60e: <div sID="gen31998" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Phil.4" sID="Phil.4"/> <div eID="gen31998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31999" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32000" type="x-p"/> Exhortations to several Christian duties, as stedfastness, unanimity, joy, &c., <reference osisRef="Phil.4.1-Phil.4.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. The apostle's grateful acknowledgments of the Philippians' kindness to him, with expressions of his own content, and desire of their good, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.10-Phil.4.19">ver. 10-19</reference>. He concludes the epistle with praise, salutations, and blessing, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.20-Phil.4.23">ver. 20-23</reference>.
entries.21f706a79d20fcb5a970efa78153754f1741b225: <div eID="gen32000" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31999" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Various Exhortations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32001" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Therefore, my brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, <hi type="italic">my</hi> dearly beloved. <hi type="super">2</hi> I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and <hi type="italic">with</hi> other my fellowlabourers, whose names <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the book of life. <hi type="super">4</hi> Rejoice in the Lord alway: <hi type="italic">and</hi> again I say, Rejoice. 5 Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> at hand. <hi type="super">6</hi> Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">8</hi> Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things <hi type="italic">are</hi> honest, whatsoever things <hi type="italic">are</hi> just, whatsoever things <hi type="italic">are</hi> pure, whatsoever things <hi type="italic">are</hi> lovely, whatsoever things <hi type="italic">are</hi> of good report; if <hi type="italic">there be</hi> any virtue, and if <hi type="italic">there be</hi> any praise, think on these things. <hi type="super">9</hi> Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you. <div eID="gen32001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32002" type="x-p"/> The apostle begins the chapter with exhortations to divers Christian duties. <div eID="gen32002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32003" type="x-p"/> I. To stedfastness in our Christian profession, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.1">v. 1</reference>. It is inferred from the close of the foregoing chapter: <hi type="italic">Therefore stand fast,</hi> &c. Seeing our <hi type="italic">conversation is in heaven,</hi> and we look for the Saviour to come thence and fetch us thither, <hi type="italic">therefore let us stand fast.</hi> Note, The believing hope and prospect of eternal life should engage us to be steady, even, and constant, in our Christian course. Observe here, <div eID="gen32003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32004" type="x-p"/> 1. The compellations are very endearing: <hi type="italic">My brethren, dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">My dearly beloved.</hi> Thus he expresses the pleasure he took in them, the kindness he had for them, to convey his exhortations to them with so much the greater advantage. He looked upon them as his brethren, though he was a great apostle. <hi type="italic">All we are brethren.</hi> There is difference of gifts, graces, and attainments, yet, being renewed by the same Spirit, after the same image, we are brethren; as the children of the same parents, though of different ages, statures, and complexions. Being brethren, (1.) He loved them, and loved them dearly: <hi type="italic">Dearly beloved;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">My dearly beloved.</hi> Warm affections become ministers and Christians towards one another. Brotherly love must always go along with brotherly relation. (2.) He loved them and longed for them, longed to see them and hear from them, longed for their welfare and was earnestly desirous of it. <hi type="italic">I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.8">ch. i. 8</reference>. (3.) He loved them and rejoiced in them. They were his joy; he had no greater joy than to hear of their spiritual health and prosperity. <hi type="italic">I rejoiced greatly that I found of thy children walking in the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2John.1.4">2 John 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="3John.1.4">3 John 4</reference>. (4.) he loved them and gloried in them. They were his crown as well as his joy. Never was proud ambitious man more pleased with the ensigns of honour than Paul was with the evidences of the sincerity of their faith and obedience. All this is to prepare his way to greater regard. <div eID="gen32004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32005" type="x-p"/> 2. The exhortation itself: <hi type="italic">So stand fast in the Lord.</hi> Being in Christ, they must stand fast in him, be even and steady in their walk with him, and close and constant unto the end. Or, To <hi type="italic">stand fast in the Lord</hi> is to stand fast in his strength and by his grace; not trusting in ourselves, and disclaiming any sufficiency of our own. We must be <hi type="italic">strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.10">Eph. vi. 10</reference>. "So stand fast, so as you have done hitherto, stand fast unto the end, so as you are by beloved, and my joy and crown; so stand fast as those in whose welfare and perseverance I am so nearly interested and concerned." <div eID="gen32005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32006" type="x-p"/> II. He exhorts them to unanimity and mutual assistance (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.2-Phil.4.3">v. 2, 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I beseech Euodias and Syntyche that they be of the same mind in the Lord.</hi> This is directed to some particular persons. Sometimes there is need of applying the general precepts of the gospel to particular persons and cases. Euodias and Syntyche, it seems, were at variance, either one with the other or with the church; either upon a civil account (it may be they were engaged in a law-suit) or upon a religious account—it may be they were of different opinions and sentiments. "Pray," says he, "desire them from me to be of the same mind in the Lord, to keep the peace and live in love, to be of the same mind one with another, not thwarting and contradicting, and to be of the same mind with the rest of the church, not acting in opposition to them." Then he exhorts to mutual assistance (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">v. 3</reference>), and this exhortation he directs to particular persons: <hi type="italic">I entreat thee also, true yoke-fellow.</hi> Who this person was whom he calls true yoke-fellow is uncertain. Some think Epaphroditus, who is supposed to have been one of the pastors of the church of the Philippians. Others think it was some eminently good woman, perhaps Paul's wife, because he exhorts his yoke-fellow to <hi type="italic">help the women who laboured with him.</hi> Whoever was the yoke-fellow with the apostle must be a yoke-fellow too with his friends. It seems, there were women who laboured with Paul in the gospel; not in the public ministry (for the apostle expressly forbids that, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.12">1 Tim. ii. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">I suffer not a woman to teach</hi>), but by entertaining the ministers, visiting the sick, instructing the ignorant, convincing the erroneous. Thus women may be helpful to ministers in the work of the gospel. Now, says the apostle, <hi type="italic">do thou help them.</hi> Those who help others should be helped themselves when there is occasion. "<hi type="italic">Help them,</hi> that is, join with them, strengthen their hands, encourage them in their difficulties."—<hi type="italic">With Clement also, and other my fellow-labourers.</hi> Paul had a kindness for all his fellow-labourers; and, as he had found the benefit of their assistance, he concluded how comfortable it would be to them to have the assistance of others. Of his fellow-labourers he says, <hi type="italic">Whose names are in the book of life;</hi> either they were chosen of God from all eternity, or registered and enrolled in the corporation and society to which the privilege of eternal life belongs, alluding to the custom among the Jews and Gentiles of registering the inhabitants or the freemen of the city. So we read of their <hi type="italic">names being written in heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Luke x. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">not blotting his name out of the book of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.5">Rev. iii. 5</reference>), and of <hi type="italic">those who are written in the Lamb's book of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">Rev. xxi. 27</reference>. Observe, There is a book of life; there are names in that book and not characters and conditions only. We cannot search into that book, or know whose names are written there; but we may, in a judgment of charity, conclude that those who labour in the gospel, and are faithful to the interest of Christ and souls, have their names in the book of life. <div eID="gen32006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32007" type="x-p"/> III. He exhorts to holy joy and delight in God: <hi type="italic">Rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, Rejoice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.4">v. 4</reference>. All our joy must terminate in God; and our thoughts of God must be delightful thoughts. <hi type="italic">Delight thyself in the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Ps. xxxvii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">in the multitude of our thoughts within us</hi> (grievous and afflicting thoughts) <hi type="italic">his comforts delight our souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.19">Ps. xciv. 19</reference>), and our <hi type="italic">meditation of him is sweet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.34">Ps. civ. 34</reference>. Observe, It is our duty and privilege to rejoice in God, and to rejoice in him always; at all times, in all conditions; even when we suffer for him, or are afflicted by him. We must not think the worse of him or of his ways for the hardships we meet with in his service. There is enough in God to furnish us with matter of joy in the worst circumstance on earth. He had said it before (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">ch. iii. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord.</hi> Here he says it again, <hi type="italic">Rejoice in the Lord always; and again I say Rejoice.</hi> Joy in God is a duty of great consequence in the Christian life; and Christians need to be again and again called to it. If good men have not a continual feast, it is their own fault. <div eID="gen32007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32008" type="x-p"/> IV. We are here exhorted to candour and gentleness, and good temper towards our brethren: "<hi type="italic">Let your moderation be known to all men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">v. 5</reference>. In things indifferent do not run into extremes; avoid bigotry and animosity; judge charitably concerning one another." The word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">to epieikes</hi></hi> signifies a good disposition towards other men; and this moderation is explained, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1-Rom.14.23">Rom. xiv</reference>. Some understand it of the patient bearing of afflictions, or the sober enjoyment of worldly good; and so it well agrees with the <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">following verse</reference>. The reason is, <hi type="italic">the Lord is at hand.</hi> The consideration of our Master's approach, and our final account, should keep us from smiting our fellow-servants, support us under present sufferings, and moderate our affections to outward good. "He will take vengeance on your enemies, and reward your patience." <div eID="gen32008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32009" type="x-p"/> V. Here is a caution against disquieting perplexing care (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be careful for nothing</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">meden merimnate</hi></hi>: the same expression with that <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Matt. vi. 25</reference>, <hi type="italic">Take no thought for your life;</hi> that is, avoid anxious care and distracting thought in the wants and difficulties of life. Observe, It is the duty and interest of Christians to live without care. There is a care of diligence which is our duty, and consists in a wise forecast and due concern; but there is a care of diffidence and distrust which is our sin and folly, and which only perplexes and distracts the mind. "<hi type="italic">Be careful for nothing,</hi> so as by your care to distrust God, and unfit yourselves for his service." <div eID="gen32009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32010" type="x-p"/> VI. As a sovereign antidote against perplexing care he recommends to us constant prayer: <hi type="italic">In every thing by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.</hi> Observe, 1. We must not only keep up stated times for prayer, but we must pray upon every particular emergency: <hi type="italic">In every thing by prayer.</hi> When any thing burdens our spirits, we must ease our minds by prayer; when our affairs are perplexed or distressed, we must seek direction and support. 2. We must join thanksgiving with our prayers and supplications. We must not only seek supplies of good, but own receipts of mercy. Grateful acknowledgments of what we have argue a right disposition of mind, and are prevailing motives for further blessings. 3. Prayer is the offering up of our desires to God, or making them known to him: <hi type="italic">Let your requests be made known to God.</hi> Not that God needs to be told either our wants or desires; for he knows them better than we can tell him: but he will know them from us, and have us show our regards and concern, express our value of the mercy and sense of our dependence on him. 4. The effect of this will be the <hi type="italic">peace of God keeping our hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">v. 7</reference>. The <hi type="italic">peace of God,</hi> that is, the comfortable sense of our reconciliation to God and interest in his favour, and the hope of the heavenly blessedness, and enjoyment of God hereafter, <hi type="italic">which passeth all understanding,</hi> is a great good than can be sufficiently valued or duly expressed. <hi type="italic">It has not entered into the heart of ham,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1 Cor. ii. 9</reference>. This peace will <hi type="italic">keep our hearts and minds through Christ Jesus;</hi> it will keep us from sinning under our troubles, and from sinking under them; keep us calm and sedate, without discomposure of passion, and with inward satisfaction. <hi type="italic">Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa. xxvi. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen32010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32011" type="x-p"/> VII. We are exhorted to get and keep a good name, a name for good things with God and good men: <hi type="italic">Whatsoever things are true and honest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">v. 8</reference>), a regard to truth in our words and engagements, and to decency and becomingness in our behaviour, suitable to our circumstances and condition of life. Whatsoever things are <hi type="italic">just and pure,</hi>—agreeable to the rules of justice and righteousness in all our dealings with men, and without the impurity or mixture of sin. Whatsoever things are <hi type="italic">lovely and of good report,</hi> that is, amiable; that will render us beloved, and make us well spoken of, as well as well thought of, by others. <hi type="italic">If there is any virtue, if there is any praise</hi>—any thing really virtuous of any kind and worthy of commendation. Observe, 1. The apostle would have the Christians learn any thing which was good of their heathen neighbours: "<hi type="italic">If there be any virtue, think of these things</hi>—imitate them in what is truly excellent among them, and let not them outdo you in any instance of goodness." We should not be ashamed to learn any good thing of bad men, or those who have not our advantages. 2. Virtue has its praise, and will have. We should walk in all the ways of virtue, and abide therein; and then, whether our praise be of men or no, it will be of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>. <div eID="gen32011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32012" type="x-p"/> In these things he proposes himself to them for an example (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those things which you have learned, and received, and heard and seen in me, do.</hi> Observe, Paul's doctrine and life were of a piece. What they saw in him was the same thing with what they heard from him. He could propose himself as well as his doctrine to their imitation. It gives a great force to what we say to others when we can appeal to what they have seen in us. And this is the way to have the <hi type="italic">God of peace with us</hi>—to keep close to our duty to him. The <hi type="italic">Lord is with us while we are with him.</hi>
entries.211f12fedae54e1c2c5f11f0fae7cc84f8623371: <div eID="gen32012" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Kindness Acknowledged; Christian Contentment. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32013" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at the last your care of me hath flourished again; wherein ye were also careful, but ye lacked opportunity. <hi type="super">11</hi> Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, <hi type="italic">therewith</hi> to be content. <hi type="super">12</hi> I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. <hi type="super">13</hi> I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. <hi type="super">14</hi> Notwithstanding ye have well done, that ye did communicate with my affliction. <hi type="super">15</hi> Now ye Philippians know also, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but ye only. <hi type="super">16</hi> For even in Thessalonica ye sent once and again unto my necessity. <hi type="super">17</hi> Not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound to your account. 18 But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things <hi type="italic">which were sent</hi> from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God. 19 But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen32013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32014" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have the thankful grateful acknowledgment which the apostle makes of the kindness of the Philippians in sending him a present for his support, now that he was a prisoner at Rome. And here, <div eID="gen32014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32015" type="x-p"/> I. He takes occasion to acknowledge their former kindnesses to him, and to make mention of them, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.15-Phil.4.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. Paul had a grateful spirit; for, though what his friends did for him was nothing in comparison of what he deserved from them and the obligations he had laid upon them, yet he speaks of their kindness as if it had been a piece of generous charity, when it was really far short of a just debt. If they had each of them contributed half their estates to him, they had not given him too much, since they <hi type="italic">owed to him even their own souls;</hi> and yet, when they send a small present to him, how kindly does he take it, how thankfully does he mention it, even in this epistle which was to be left upon record, and read in the churches, through all ages; so that wherever this epistle shall be read there shall this which they did to Paul be told for a memorial of them. Surely never was present so well repaid. He reminds them that <hi type="italic">in the beginning of the gospel no church communicated with him as to giving and receiving but they only,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">v. 15</reference>. They not only maintained him comfortably while he was with them, but when <hi type="italic">he departed from Macedonia</hi> they sent tokens of their kindness after him; and this when no other church did so. None besides sent after him of their carnal things, in consideration of what they had reaped of his spiritual things. In works of charity, we are ready to ask what other people do. But the church of the Philippians never considered that. It redounded so much the more to their honour that they were the only church who were thus just and generous. <hi type="italic">Even in Thessalonica</hi> (after he had departed from Macedonia) <hi type="italic">you sent once and again to my necessity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">v. 16</reference>. Observe, 1. It was but little which they sent; they sent only to his necessity, just such things as he had need of; perhaps it was according to their ability, and he did not desire superfluities nor dainties. 2. It is an excellent thing to see those to whom God has abounded in the gifts of his grace abounding in grateful returns to his people and ministers, according to their own ability and their necessity: <hi type="italic">You sent once and again.</hi> Many people make it an excuse for their charity that they have given once; why should the charge come upon them again? But the Philippians sent once and again; they often relieved and refreshed him in his necessities. He makes this mention of their former kindness, not only out of gratitude, but for their encouragement. <div eID="gen32015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32016" type="x-p"/> II. He excuses their neglect of late. It seems, for some time they had not sent to enquire after him, or sent him any present; but <hi type="italic">now at the last their care of him flourished again</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.10">v. 10</reference>), like a tree in the spring, which seemed all the winter to be quite dead. Now, in conformity to the example of his great Master, instead of upbraiding them for their neglect, he makes an excuse for them: <hi type="italic">Wherein you were also careful, but you lacked opportunity.</hi> How could they lack opportunity, if they had been resolved upon it? They might have sent a messenger on purpose. But the apostle is willing to suppose, in favour of them, that they would have done it if a fair opportunity had offered. How contrary is this to the behaviour of many to their friends, by whom neglects which really are excusable are resented very heinously, when Paul excused that which he had reason enough to resent. <div eID="gen32016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32017" type="x-p"/> III. He commends their present liberality: <hi type="italic">Notwithstanding, you have well done that you did communicate with my affliction,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.14">v. 14</reference>. It is a good work to succour and help a good minister in trouble. Here see what is the nature of true Christian sympathy; not only to be concerned for our friends in their troubles, but to do what we can to help them. They <hi type="italic">communicated with his affliction,</hi> in relieving him under it. He who says, <hi type="italic">Be you warmed, be you filled, and giveth not those things they have need of, what doth it profit?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.16">Jam. ii. 16</reference>. He rejoiced greatly in it (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.10">v. 10</reference>), because it was an evidence of their affection to him and the success of his ministry among them. When the fruit of their charity abounded towards the apostle, it appeared that the fruit of his ministry abounded among them. <div eID="gen32017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32018" type="x-p"/> IV. He takes care to obviate the bad use some might make of his taking so much notice of what was sent him. It did not proceed either from discontent and distrust (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.11">v. 11</reference>) or from covetousness and love of the world, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">v. 12</reference>. 1. It did not come from discontent, or distrust of Providence: <hi type="italic">Not that I speak in respect of want</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.11">v. 11</reference>); not in respect of any want he felt, nor of any want he feared. As to the former, he was content with the little he had, and that satisfied him; as to the latter, he depended upon the providence of God to provide for him from day to day, and that satisfied him: so that he did not speak in respect of want any way. <hi type="italic">For I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.</hi> We have here an account of Paul's learning, not that which he got at the feet of Gamaliel, but that which he got at the feet of Christ. He had learnt to be content; and that was the lesson he had as much need to learn as most men, considering the hardships and sufferings with which he was exercised. He was in bonds, and imprisonments, and necessities, often; but in all he had learnt to be content, that is, to bring his mind to his condition, and make the best of it.—<hi type="italic">I know both how to be abased and I know how to abound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">v. 12</reference>. This is a special act of grace, to accommodate ourselves to every condition of life, and carry an equal temper of mind through all the varieties of our state. (1.) To accommodate ourselves to an afflicted condition—to know how to be abased, how to be hungry, how to suffer want, so as not to be overcome by the temptations of it, either to lose our comfort in God or distrust his providence, or to take any indirect course for our own supply. (2.) To a prosperous condition—to know how to abound, how to be full, so as not to be proud, or secure, or luxurious. And this is as hard a lesson as the other; for the temptations of fulness and prosperity are not less than those of affliction and want. But how must we learn it? <hi type="italic">I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.13">v. 13</reference>. We have need of strength from Christ, to enable us to perform not only those duties which are purely Christian, but even those which are the fruit of moral virtue. We need his strength to teach us to be content in every condition. The apostle had seemed to boast of himself, and of his own strength: <hi type="italic">I know how to be abased</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">v. 12</reference>); but here he transfers all the praise to Christ. "What do I talk of <hi type="italic">knowing how to be abased, and how to abound?</hi> It is only <hi type="italic">through Christ who strengthens me</hi> that I can do it, not in my own strength." So we are required to be <hi type="italic">strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.10">Eph. vi. 10</reference>), and to be <hi type="italic">strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1">2 Tim. ii. 1</reference>); and we are <hi type="italic">strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16">Eph. iii. 16</reference>. The word in the original is a participle of the present tense, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en to endynamounti me Christo,</hi></hi> and denotes a present and continued act; as if he had said, "Through Christ, who is strengthening me, and does continually strengthen me; it is by his constant and renewed strength I am enabled to act in every thing; I wholly depend upon him for all my spiritual power." 2. It did not come from covetousness, or an affection to worldly wealth: "<hi type="italic">Not because I desired a gift</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.17">v. 17</reference>): that is, I welcome your kindness, not because it adds to my enjoyments, but because it adds to your account." He desired not so much for his own sake, but theirs: <hi type="italic">"I desire fruit that may abound to your account,</hi> that is, that you may be enabled to make such a good use of your worldly possessions that you may give an account of them with joy." It is not with any design to draw more from you, but to encourage you to such an exercise of beneficence as will meet with a glorious reward hereafter. "For my part," says he, "<hi type="italic">I have all, and abound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">v. 18</reference>. What can a man desire more than enough? I do not desire a gift for the gift's sake, for <hi type="italic">I have all, and abound.</hi>" They sent him a small token, and he desired no more; he was not solicitous for a present superfluity, or a future supply: <hi type="italic">I am full, having received from Epaphroditus the things which were sent by you.</hi> Note, A good man will soon have enough of this world; not only of living in it, but of receiving from it. A covetous worldling, if he has ever so much, would still have more; but a heavenly Christian, though he has little, has enough. <div eID="gen32018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32019" type="x-p"/> V. The apostle assures them that God did accept, and would recompense, their kindness to him. 1. He did accept it: <hi type="italic">It is an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, well-pleasing to God.</hi> Not a sacrifice of atonement, for none makes atonement for sin but Christ; but a sacrifice of acknowledgment, and <hi type="italic">well-pleasing to God.</hi> It was more acceptable to God as it was the fruit of their grace than it was to Paul as it was the supply of his want. <hi type="italic">With such sacrifices God is well pleased,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.16">Heb. xiii. 16</reference>. 2. He would recompense it: <hi type="italic">But my God shall supply all your wants according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.19">v. 19</reference>. He does as it were draw a bill upon the exchequer in heaven, and leaves it to God to make them amends for the kindness they had shown him. "He shall do it, not only as your God, but as my God, who takes what is done to me as done to himself. You supplied my needs, according to your poverty; and he shall supply yours, according to his riches." But still it is by Christ Jesus; through him we have grace to do that which is good, and through him we must expect the reward of it. Not of debt, but of grace; for the more we do for God the more we are indebted to him, because we receive the more from him.
entries.106ec21ef74ac62f007271e5ac92cbf8806ee73e: <div eID="gen32019" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conclusion. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32020" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Now unto God and our Father <hi type="italic">be</hi> glory for ever and ever. Amen. <hi type="super">21</hi> Salute every saint in Christ Jesus. The brethren which are with me greet you. <hi type="super">22</hi> All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Cæsar's household. 23 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you all. Amen. <div eID="gen32020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32021" type="x-p"/> The apostle concludes the epistle in these verses, <div eID="gen32021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32022" type="x-p"/> 1. With praises to God: <hi type="italic">Now unto God and our Father be glory for ever and ever, Amen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.20">v. 20</reference>. Observe, (1.) God is to be considered by us as our Father: <hi type="italic">Now unto God and our Father.</hi> It is a great condescension and favour in God to own the relation of Father to sinners, and allow us to say to him, <hi type="italic">Our Father;</hi> and it is a title peculiar to the gospel dispensation. It is also a great privilege and encouragement to us to consider him as our Father, as one so nearly related and who bears so tender an affection towards us. We should look upon God, under all our weaknesses and fears, not as a tyrant or an enemy, but as a Father, who is disposed to pity us and help us. (2.) We must ascribe glory to God as a Father, the glory of his own excellence and of all his mercy unto us. We must thankfully own the receipt of all from him, and give the praise of all to him. And our praise must be constant and perpetual; it must be <hi type="italic">glory for ever and ever.</hi> <div eID="gen32022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32023" type="x-p"/> 2. With salutations to his friends at Philippi: "<hi type="italic">Salute every saint in Christ Jesus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.21">v. 21</reference>); give my hearty love to all the Christians in your parts." He desires remembrances not only to the bishops and deacons, and the church in general, but to every particular saint. Paul had a kind affection to all good Christians. <div eID="gen32023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32024" type="x-p"/> 3. He sends salutations from those who were at Rome: "<hi type="italic">The brethren who are with me salute you;</hi> the <hi type="italic">ministers,</hi> and all the saints here, send their affectionate remembrances to you. <hi type="italic">Chiefly those who are of Cæsar's household;</hi> the Christian converts who belonged to the emperor's court." Observe, (1.) There were saints in Cæsar's household. Though Paul was imprisoned at Rome, for preaching the gospel, by the emperor's command, yet there were some Christians in his own family. The gospel early obtained among some of the rich and great. Perhaps the apostle fared the better, and received some favour, by means of his friends at court. (2.) <hi type="italic">Chiefly those,</hi> &c. Observe, They, being bred at court, were more complaisant than the rest. See what an ornament to religion sanctified civility is. <div eID="gen32024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32025" type="x-p"/> 4. The apostolical benediction, as usual: "<hi type="italic">The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, Amen.</hi> The free favour and good will of Christ be your portion and happiness."  <chapter eID="Phil.4"/> <div eID="gen32025" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen31906" osisID="Phil" type="book"/>

entries.606a8331c6ad6d5658e310e6f7fa3640cb8f4080: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17802"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Phil.4.1-Phil.4.23">Php 4:1-23</reference>. Exhortations: Thanks for the Supply from Philippi:</title> <div sID="gen36113" type="x-p"/> Greeting; and Closing Benediction.<div eID="gen36113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17802"/>1. "Wherefore"; since we have such a glorious hope (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen36114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dearly beloved--</hi>repeated again at the close of the verse, implying that his great love to them should be a motive to their obedience.<div eID="gen36115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">longed for--</hi>"yearned after" in your absence (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.8">Php 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crown--</hi>in the day of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.16">Php 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen36117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so--</hi>as I have admonished you.<div eID="gen36118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand fast--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Phil.1.27">Php 1:27</reference>). <div eID="gen36119" type="x-p"/>
entries.4527e9cfc07c26142907002d9cd4d75589939333: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17803"/><div sID="gen36120" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17803"/>2. Euodia and Syntyche were two women who seem to have been at variance; probably deaconesses of the church. He repeats, "I beseech," as if he would admonish each separately, and with the utmost impartiality.<div eID="gen36120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord--</hi>the true element of Christian union; for those "in the Lord" by faith to be at variance, is an utter inconsistency. <div eID="gen36121" type="x-p"/>
entries.767b3fe161a8e5b43116bb2db4e331db996441d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17804"/><div sID="gen36122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17804"/><hi type="bold">3. And--</hi>Greek, "Yea."<div eID="gen36122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">true yoke-fellow--</hi>yoked with me in the same Gospel yoke (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">30</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Ti 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">18</reference>). Either Timothy, Silas (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.40">Ac 15:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.19">16:19</reference>, at Philippi), or the chief bishop of Philippi. Or else the Greek, "Sunzugus," or "Synzygus," is a proper name: "Who art truly, as thy name means, a yoke-fellow." Certainly not Paul's wife, as <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.5">1Co 9:5</reference> implies he had none.<div eID="gen36123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">help those women--</hi>rather, as Greek, "help them," namely, Euodia and Syntyche. "Co-operate with them" [Birks]; or as Alford, "Help in the work of their reconciliation."<div eID="gen36124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which laboured with me--</hi>"inasmuch as they labored with me." At Philippi, women were the first hearers of the Gospel, and Lydia the first convert. It is a coincidence which marks genuineness, that in this Epistle alone, special instructions are given to women who labored with Paul in the Gospel. In selecting the first teachers, those first converted would naturally be fixed on. Euodia and Syntyche were doubtless two of "the women who resorted to the riverside, where prayer was wont to be made" (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.13">Ac 16:13</reference>), and being early converted, would naturally take an active part in teaching other women called at a later period; of course not in public preaching, but in a less prominent sphere (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen36125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Clement--</hi>bishop of Rome shortly after the death of Peter and Paul. His Epistle from the Church of Rome to the Church of Corinth is extant. It makes no mention of the supremacy of the See of Peter. He was the most eminent of the apostolical fathers. Alford thinks that the Clement here was a Philippian, and not necessarily Clement, bishop of Rome. But Origen [Commentary, John 1:29] identifies the Clement here with the bishop of Rome.<div eID="gen36126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the book of life--</hi>the register-book of those whose "citizenship is in heaven" (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Lu 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>). Anciently, free cities had a roll book containing the names of all those having the right of citizenship (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.32.32">Ex 32:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.28">Psa 69:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.9">Eze 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">21:27</reference>). <div eID="gen36127" type="x-p"/>
entries.3fbd11f008fae18a2d8a2e5070c53338b7302050: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17805"/><div sID="gen36128" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17805"/>4. (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>.)<div eID="gen36128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36129" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alway--</hi>even amidst the afflictions now distressing you (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.28-Phil.1.30">Php 1:28-30</reference>).<div eID="gen36129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">again--</hi>as he had already said, "Rejoice" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Php 3:1</reference>). Joy is the predominant feature of the Epistle.<div eID="gen36130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36131" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I say--</hi>Greek, rather, "I will say." <div eID="gen36131" type="x-p"/>
entries.31bb95472c6e2de8badb83a13ff1fe5ad44c510a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17806"/><div sID="gen36132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17806"/><hi type="bold">5. moderation--</hi>from a Greek root, "to yield," whence yieldingness [Trench]; or from a root, "it is fitting," whence "reasonableness of dealing" [Alford], that considerateness for others, not urging one's own rights to the uttermost, but waiving a part, and thereby rectifying the injustices of justice. The archetype of this grace is God, who presses not the strictness of His law against us as we deserve (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.3">Psa 130:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">4</reference>); though having exacted the fullest payment for us from our Divine Surety. There are included in "moderation," candor and kindliness. Joy in the Lord raises us above rigorism towards others (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Php 4:5</reference>), and carefulness (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>) as to one's own affairs. Sadness produces morose harshness towards others, and a troublesome spirit in ourselves.<div eID="gen36132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let ... be known--</hi>that is, in your conduct to others, let nothing inconsistent with "moderation" be seen. Not a precept to make a display of moderation. Let this grace "be known" to men in acts; let "your requests be made to God" in word (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto all men--</hi>even to the "perverse" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.15">Php 2:15</reference>), that so ye may win them. Exercise "forbearance" even to your persecutors. None is so ungracious as not to be kindly to someone, from some motive or another, on some occasion; the believer is to be so "unto all men" at all times.<div eID="gen36134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The Lord is at hand--</hi>The Lord's coming again speedily is the grand motive to every Christian grace (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.8">Jas 5:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.9">9</reference>). Harshness to others (the opposite of "moderation") would be taking into our own hands prematurely the prerogatives of judging, which belongs to the Lord alone (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>); and so provoking God to judge us by the strict letter of the law (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.12">Jas 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen36135" type="x-p"/>
entries.22ba26baf6d5fdeece9e0350cf2fed1ac897418f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17807"/><div sID="gen36136" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17807"/>6. Translate, "Be anxious about nothing." Care and prayer are as mutually opposed as fire and water [Bengel].<div eID="gen36136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by prayer and supplication--</hi>Greek, "by the prayer and the supplication" appropriate to each case [Alford]. Prayer for blessings; and the general term. Supplication, to avert ills; a special term, suppliant entreaty (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.6.18">Ep 6:18</reference>).<div eID="gen36137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thanksgiving--</hi>for every event, prosperity and affliction alike (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.18">1Th 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jas 5:13</reference>). The Philippians might remember Paul's example at Philippi when in the innermost prison (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.25">Ac 16:25</reference>). Thanksgiving gives effect to prayer (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Ch 20:21</reference>), and frees from anxious carefulness by making all God's dealings matter for praise, not merely for resignation, much less murmuring. "Peace" is the companion of "thanksgiving" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Php 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let your requests be made known unto God--</hi>with generous, filial, unreserved confidence; not keeping aught back, as too great, or else too small, to bring before God, though you might feel so as to your fellow men. So Jacob, when fearing Esau (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.9-Gen.32.12">Ge 32:9-12</reference>); Hezekiah fearing Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14">2Ki 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5">Psa 37:5</reference>). <div eID="gen36139" type="x-p"/>
entries.617f76337120974f2d22ce83fc3b40186120a2ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17808"/><div sID="gen36140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17808"/><hi type="bold">7. And--</hi>The inseparable consequence of thus laying everything before God in "prayer with thanksgiving."<div eID="gen36140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace--</hi>the dispeller of "anxious care" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>coming from God, and resting in God (<reference osisRef="John.14.27">Joh 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.33">16:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36143" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passeth--</hi>surpasseth, or exceedeth, all man's notional powers of understanding its full blessedness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Ep 3:20</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Prov.3.17">Pr 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen36143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall keep--</hi>rather, "shall guard"; shall keep as a well-garrisoned stronghold (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Is 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">3</reference>). The same Greek verb is used in <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1Pe 1:5</reference>. There shall be peace secure within, whatever outward troubles may besiege.<div eID="gen36144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hearts and minds--</hi>rather, "hearts (the seat of the thoughts) and thoughts" or purposes.<div eID="gen36145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>rather as Greek, "in Christ Jesus." It is in Christ that we are "kept" or "guarded" secure. <div eID="gen36146" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc7e9cf00ee4825cf965630b5a0fc072140c42f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17809"/><div sID="gen36147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17809"/>8. Summary of all his exhortations as to relative duties, whether as children or parents, husbands or wives, friends, neighbors, men in the intercourse of the world, &c.<div eID="gen36147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">true--</hi>sincere, in words.<div eID="gen36148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honest--</hi>Old English for "seemly," namely, in action; literally, grave, dignified.<div eID="gen36149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">just--</hi>towards others.<div eID="gen36150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pure--</hi>"chaste," in relation to ourselves.<div eID="gen36151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lovely--</hi>lovable (compare <reference osisRef="Mark.10.21">Mr 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.7.4">Lu 7:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen36152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of good report--</hi>referring to the absent (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.27">Php 1:27</reference>); as "lovely" refers to what is lovable face to face.<div eID="gen36153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if there be any virtue--</hi>"whatever virtue there is" [Alford]. "Virtue," the standing word in heathen ethics, is found once only in Paul's Epistles, and once in Peter's (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.5">2Pe 1:5</reference>); and this in uses different from those in heathen authors. It is a term rather earthly and human, as compared with the names of the spiritual graces which Christianity imparts; hence the rarity of its occurrence in the New Testament. Piety and true morality are inseparable. Piety is love with its face towards God; morality is love with its face towards man. Despise not anything that is good in itself; only let it keep its due place.<div eID="gen36154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">praise--</hi>whatever is praiseworthy; not that Christians should make man's praise their aim (compare <reference osisRef="John.12.43">Joh 12:43</reference>); but they should live so as to deserve men's praise.<div eID="gen36155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think on--</hi>have a continual regard to, so as to "do" these things (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.9">Php 4:9</reference>) whenever the occasion arises. <div eID="gen36156" type="x-p"/>
entries.33479fdc04913da20b3ebb5669344c936004b23b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17810"/><div sID="gen36157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17810"/><hi type="bold">9. both--</hi>rather, "The things also which ye have learned ... these practice"; the things which besides recommending them in words, have been also recommended by my example, carry into practice.<div eID="gen36157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard--</hi>though ye have not yet sufficiently "received" them.<div eID="gen36158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen--</hi>though ye have not as yet sufficiently "learned" them [Bengel].<div eID="gen36159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>"and then," as the necessary result (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Php 4:7</reference>). Not only "the peace of God," but "the God of peace" Himself "shall be with you." <div eID="gen36160" type="x-p"/>
entries.10e2ddd294a7b62da582bc34e32f393e6d6a499a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17811"/><div sID="gen36161" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17811"/><hi type="bold">10. But--</hi>transitional conjunction. But "now" to pass to another subject.<div eID="gen36161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord--</hi>He views everything with reference to Christ.<div eID="gen36162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the last--</hi>"at last"; implying he was expecting their gift, not from a selfish view, but as a "fruit" of their faith, and to "abound" to their account (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.11">Php 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.17">17</reference>). Though long in coming, owing to Epaphroditus' sickness and other delays, he does not imply their gift was too late.<div eID="gen36163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your care ... hath flourished again--</hi>Greek, "Ye have flourished again (revived, as trees sprouting forth again in spring) in your care for me."<div eID="gen36164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein ye were also careful--</hi>in respect to which (revival, namely, the sending of a supply to me) "ye were also (all along) careful, but ye lacked opportunity"; whether from want of means or want of a messenger. Your "lack of service" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.30">Php 2:30</reference>), was owing to your having "lacked opportunity." <div eID="gen36165" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d26b73f0de362e5897719fa0856b01b398dcc04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17812"/><div sID="gen36166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17812"/><hi type="bold">11. I have learned--</hi>The I in Greek is emphatical. I leave it to others if they will, to be discontented. I, for my part, have learned, by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, and the dealings of Providence (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.8">He 5:8</reference>), to be content in every state.<div eID="gen36166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">content--</hi>The Greek, literally expresses "independent of others, and having sufficiency in one's self." But Christianity has raised the term above the haughty self-sufficiency of the heathen Stoic to the contentment of the Christian, whose sufficiency is not in self, but in God (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2Co 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6">1Ti 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5">He 13:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.36">Jr 2:36</reference>; 45:5). <div eID="gen36167" type="x-p"/>
entries.5798284471498c3a83718eb588dbf1cc3b2bcbcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17813"/><div sID="gen36168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17813"/><hi type="bold">12. abased--</hi>in low circumstances (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8">2Co 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.9">6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen36168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everywhere--</hi>rather, "in each, and in all things" [Alford].<div eID="gen36169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">instructed--</hi>in the secret. Literally, "initiated" in a secret teaching, which is a mystery unknown to the world. <div eID="gen36170" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8a1da5ba2402948ff256001c7a147904a3977e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17814"/><div sID="gen36171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17814"/><hi type="bold">13. I can do all things--</hi>Greek, "I have strength for all things"; not merely "how to be abased and how to abound." After special instances he declares his universal power--how triumphantly, yet how humbly! [Meyer].<div eID="gen36171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through Christ which strengtheneth me--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "Christ"; then translate, "In Him who giveth me power," that is, by virtue of my living union and identification with Him, who is my strength (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12">1Ti 1:12</reference>, whence probably, "Christ" was inserted here by transcribers. <div eID="gen36172" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccc538a097631061ef0c5e1bd967c22cd961a44f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17815"/><div sID="gen36173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17815"/>14. He here guards against their thinking from what he has just said, that he makes light of their bounty.<div eID="gen36173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye did communicate with my affliction--</hi>that is, ye made yourselves sharers with me in my present affliction, namely, by sympathy; of which sympathy your contribution is the proof. <div eID="gen36174" type="x-p"/>
entries.07b8177bf82988121ed3d50c023945bbff865b9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17816"/><div sID="gen36175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17816"/><hi type="bold">15. Now--</hi>"Moreover." Arrange as Greek, "Ye also know (as well as I do myself)."<div eID="gen36175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the beginning of the gospel--</hi>dating from the Philippian Christian era; at the first preaching of the Gospel at Philippi.<div eID="gen36176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I departed from Macedonia--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.17.14">Ac 17:14</reference>). The Philippians had followed Paul with their bounty when he left Macedonia and came to Corinth. <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.8">2Co 11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">9</reference> thus accords with the passage here, the dates assigned to the donation in both Epistles agreeing; namely, "in the beginning of the Gospel" here, and there, at the time of his first visit to Corinth [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ]. However, the supply meant here is not that which he received at Corinth, but the supply sent to him when "in Thessalonica, once and again" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">Php 4:16</reference>), [Alford].<div eID="gen36177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as concerning giving and receiving--</hi>In the account between us, "the giving" was all on your part; "the receiving" all on mine.<div eID="gen36178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye only--</hi>We are not to wait for others in a good work, saying, "I will do so, when others do it." We must go forward, though alone. <div eID="gen36179" type="x-p"/>
entries.8368131e6eebbd517c7139cc5a7412e159cc8245: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17817"/><div sID="gen36180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17817"/><hi type="bold">16. even in Thessalonica--</hi>"even" as early as when I had got no further than Thessalonica, ye sent me supplies for my necessities more than once. <div eID="gen36180" type="x-p"/>
entries.c97ee4f65e28cc4899176a1523f1c7a929bcc752: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17818"/><div sID="gen36181" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17818"/><hi type="bold">17. a gift--</hi>Greek, "the gift." Translate, "It is not that I seek after the gift, but I do seek after the fruit that aboundeth to your account"; what I do seek is your spiritual good, in the abounding of fruits of your faith which shall be put down to your account, against the day of reward (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">He 6:10</reference>). <div eID="gen36181" type="x-p"/>
entries.63e636ad83372f8deeb8f3c6e5a822c39195d18f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17819"/><div sID="gen36182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17819"/><hi type="bold">18. But--</hi>Though "the gift" is not what I chiefly "seek after" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.17">Php 4:17</reference>), yet I am grateful for the gift, and hereby acknowledge it as ample for all my needs. Translate, "I have all" that I want, "and more than enough." Literally, as English Version, "I abound" over and above my needs.<div eID="gen36182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am full--</hi>Greek, "I am filled full."<div eID="gen36183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the odour of a sweet smell--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>). The figure is drawn from the sweet-smelling incense which was burnt along with the sacrifices; their gift being in faith was not so much to Paul, as to God (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.40">Mt 25:40</reference>), before whom it "came up for a memorial" (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.4">Ac 10:4</reference>), sweet-smelling in God's presence (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Ge 8:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Re 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen36184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sacrifice acceptable--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.13.16">He 13:16</reference>). <div eID="gen36185" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9072b61fb45f4ab816b4373c0618182032bad97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17820"/><div sID="gen36186" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17820"/><hi type="bold">19. my--</hi>Paul calls God here "my God," to imply that God would reward their bounty to His servant, by "fully supplying" (translate so, literally, fill to the full) their every "need" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.8">2Co 9:8</reference>), even as they had "fully" supplied his "need" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">Php 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">18</reference>). My Master will fully repay you; I cannot. The Philippians invested their bounty well since it got them such a glorious return.<div eID="gen36186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to his riches--</hi>The measure of His supply to you will be the immeasurable "riches of His grace" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen36187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in glory--</hi>These words belong to the whole sentence. "Glory" is the element in which His rich grace operates; and it will be the element IN which He will "supply fully all your need."<div eID="gen36188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by Christ Jesus--</hi>by virtue of your being "IN" (so Greek, not "by") Christ Jesus, the Giver and Mediator of all spiritual blessings. <div eID="gen36189" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a5552e575da574691683aa798b8df9aa8131b67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17821"/><div sID="gen36190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17821"/><hi type="bold">20. God and our Father--</hi>Translate, "Unto our God and Father."<div eID="gen36190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be glory--</hi>rather as the Greek, "be the glory." Not to us, but to Him be "the glory" alike of your gift, and of His gracious recompense to you. <div eID="gen36191" type="x-p"/>
entries.868e1a5fcbc56db6ed2fa9db12afa9b3aec1f2b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17822"/><div sID="gen36192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17822"/><hi type="bold">21. Salute every saint--</hi>individually.<div eID="gen36192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">greet--</hi>salute you.<div eID="gen36193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The brethren which are with me--</hi>Perhaps Jewish believers are meant (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.21">Ac 28:21</reference>). I think <reference osisRef="Phil.2.20">Php 2:20</reference> precludes our thinking of "closer friends," "colleagues in the ministry" [Alford]; he had only one close friend with him, namely, Timothy. <div eID="gen36194" type="x-p"/>
entries.c74f354580526e953b4d753aa118c01ab23fddb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17823"/><div sID="gen36195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17823"/><hi type="bold">22. they that are of Cæsar's household--</hi>the slaves and dependents of Nero who had been probably converted through Paul's teaching while he was a prisoner in the Prætorian barrack attached to the palace. Philippi was a Roman "colony," hence there might arise a tie between the citizens of the mother city and those of the colony; especially between those of both cities who were Christians, converted as many of them were by the same apostle, and under like circumstances, he having been imprisoned at Philippi, as he now is at Rome. <div eID="gen36195" type="x-p"/>
entries.df37da6c649cee22fa78b6cd0a7d12b8c4df12ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17824"/><div sID="gen36196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17824"/>23. (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.18">Ga 6:18</reference>).<div eID="gen36196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be with you all. Amen--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Be with your spirit," and omit "Amen." <chapter eID="Phil.4"/><div eID="gen36197" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen35863" osisID="Phil" type="book"/>

entries.8100995b82e19f1a8fcd58fdde3be2d57c9bbaf4: <div eID="gen50691" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen50692" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50693" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50693" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50692" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50694" type="x-p"/> The apostle exhorts them to stand fast in the Lord, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.1">Phi 4:1</reference>. And beseeches Euodias and Syntyche to be of one mind in Divine things, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.2">Phi 4:2</reference>. And requests his true yokefellow to help them to a good understanding, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.3">Phi 4:3</reference>. Gives them directions concerning their temper and frame of mind, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.4-Phi.4.7">Phi 4:4-7</reference>. And how to act in all respects as becomes the purity and excellence of the Gospel, as they had heard from and seen in him, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.8">Phi 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.9">Phi 4:9</reference>. Thanks them for their attention to him in his captivity, in sending him what was necessary for his support, though he had learned to be contented in all situations in life, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.10-Phi.4.14">Phi 4:10-14</reference>. Mentions particular cases in which they had ministered to him; promises them, through the riches of glory in Christ, a supply of all their spiritual wants; and renders thanks to God, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.15-Phi.4.20">Phi 4:15-20</reference>. Salutes all the saints, and those particularly of the emperor's household, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.21">Phi 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.22">Phi 4:22</reference>. And concludes with his usual apostolical benediction, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.23">Phi 4:23</reference>. <div eID="gen50694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50695" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen50695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50696" type="x-p"/> Therefore, my - beloved - Because ye have this armor, and those enemies, and God for your support, see that ye stand fast in him. This verse most unquestionably belongs to the preceding chapter.
entries.be49c0255851aa264f9dba0a2ac6b8f3cbaaa9e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen50696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50697" type="x-p"/> I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche - These were two pious women, as it is generally supposed, who were deaconesses in the Church at Philippi, and who in some points of doctrine and discipline had disagreed. He exhorts them to be of the same mind, that is, to compose their differences; and, if they could not perfectly agree to think and let think, and to avoid all public opposition, as their dissension would strengthen the hands of the common enemy, and stumble those who were weak. But it is more likely that Euodias was a woman, and Syntyche a man, and probably the husband of Euodias; and that it is Syntyche whom the apostle calls true yokefellow in the next verse.
entries.00d872c5e1615830d3ae4aa0dc49dae39e90690a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen50697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50698" type="x-p"/> Help those women which labored with me - Both in the Grecian and Asiatic countries women were kept much secluded, and is was not likely that even the apostles had much opportunity of conversing with them; it was therefore necessary that they should have some experienced Christian women with them, who could have access to families, and preach Jesus to the female part of them. The apostle tells us that certain women labored with him in the Gospel, and were assistants to others also who had assisted him. <div eID="gen50698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50699" type="x-p"/> Some think the women here were Euodias and Syntyche; but I rather incline to the opinion that Syntyche was a male, and Euodias his wife. Euodias signifies a pleasant scent; Syntyche, fortunate. There have been a number of conjectures who these persons were, and who is meant by the true yokefellow; but as there is nothing certain known on the subject, it is useless to propagate conjecture. <div eID="gen50699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50700" type="x-p"/> With Clement also - Supposed to be the same who was afterwards bishop of Rome, and who wrote an epistle to the Corinthians, which is still extant. <div eID="gen50700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50701" type="x-p"/> Whose names are in the book of life - Who are genuine Christians; who are enlisted or enrolled in the armies of the Lord, and have received a title to eternal glory. The reader is requested to refer to the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.32.32-Exo.32.33">Exo 32:32-33</reference> (note), and the concluding observations at the end of that chapter, (<reference osisRef="Exo.32.35">Exo 32:35</reference> (note)) where the writing in and blotting out of the book of life are particularly considered, and the difficulties on the subject removed. See also on <reference osisRef="Luk.10.20">Luk 10:20</reference> (note).
entries.ede998e604fb3a69872425171255de37b7911bf7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen50701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50702" type="x-p"/> Rejoice in the Lord alway - Be continually happy; but this happiness you can find only in the Lord. Genuine happiness is spiritual; as it can only come from God, so it infallibly tends to him. The apostle repeats the exhortation, to show, not only his earnestness, but also that it was God's will that it should be so, and that it was their duty as well as interest.
entries.4cd09630c2c54dba3aaadcfecad3ea24176cc79f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen50702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50703" type="x-p"/> Let your moderation be known - The word επιεικες is of very extensive signification; it means the same as επιεικεια, mildness, patience, yieldingness, gentleness, clemency, moderation, unwillingness to litigate or contend; but moderation is expressive enough as a general term. "Moderation," says Dr. Macknight, "means meekness under provocation, readiness to forgive injuries, equity in the management of business, candour in judging of the characters and actions of others, sweetness of disposition, and the entire government of the passions." <div eID="gen50703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50704" type="x-p"/> The Lord is at hand - A phrase something similar to the Maranatha of <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.22">1Cor 16:22</reference> : The Lord is Judge, and is at hand to punish. Schoettgen supposes, from this verse, taken in connection with the preceding, that Euodias and Syntyche were of a quarrelsome disposition; and hence the exhortation and threatening in the third and fifth verses.
entries.04159b3af8dcdcd1e1451695abc8af7b8997ea96: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen50704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50705" type="x-p"/> Be careful for nothing - Μηδεν μεριμνατε· Be not anxiously solicitous; do not give place to carking care, let what will occur; for anxiety cannot chance the state or condition of any thing from bad to good, but will infallibly injure your own souls. <div eID="gen50705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50706" type="x-p"/> By prayer and supplication - God alone can help you; he is disposed to do it, but you must ask by prayer and supplication; without this he has not promised to help you. <div eID="gen50706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50707" type="x-p"/> By prayer - solemn application to God from a sense of want. <div eID="gen50707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50708" type="x-p"/> Supplication - continuance in earnest prayer. With thanksgiving, for innumerable favors already received; and for dangers, evils, and deaths turned aside. And let your souls be found in this exercise, or in the disposition in which this exercise can be performed, at all times, on all occasions, and in all places.
entries.1d226b90b937e31c022079eeb12ef3873a96674c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen50708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50709" type="x-p"/> And the peace of God - That harmonizing of all passions and appetites which is produced by the Holy Spirit, and arises from a sense of pardon and the favor of God; <div eID="gen50709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50710" type="x-p"/> Shall keep your hearts - Φρουρησει· Shall keep them as in a strong place or castle. Your hearts - the seat of all your affections and passions, and minds - your understanding, judgment, and conscience through Christ Jesus; by whom ye were brought into this state of favor, through whom ye are preserved in it, and in whom ye possess it; for Christ keeps that heart in peace in which he dwells and rules. This peace passeth all understanding; it is of a very different nature from all that can arise from human occurrences; it is a peace which Christ has purchased, and which God dispenses; it is felt by all the truly godly, but can be explained by none; it is communion with the Father, and his Son Jesus Christ, by the power and influence of the Holy Ghost.
entries.4c5dd3015921710151552fc65788af0653e1c123: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen50710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50711" type="x-p"/> Finally, brethren - The object of the apostle is to recommend holiness and righteousness to them in every point of view; and to show that the Gospel of Christ requires all its professors to have the mind that was in Christ, and to walk as he himself also walked. That they were not to attend to one branch of righteousness or virtue only, but to every thing by which they might bring honor to God, good to their fellow creatures, and credit to themselves. <div eID="gen50711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50712" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever things are true - Ὁσα - αληθη· All that is agreeable to unchangeable and eternal truth. Whether that which is to be learned from the nature and state of created things, or that which comes immediately from God by revelation. <div eID="gen50712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50713" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever things are honest - Ὁσα σεμνα· Whatever is grave, decent, and venerable. Whatever becomes you as men, as citizens, and as Christians. <div eID="gen50713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50714" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever things are just - Ὁσα δικαια· Whatsoever is agreeable to justice and righteousness. All that ye owe to God, to your neighbor, and to yourselves. <div eID="gen50714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50715" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever things are pure - Ὁσα ἁγνα· Whatsoever is chaste. In reference to the state of the mind, and to the acts of the body. <div eID="gen50715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50716" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever things are lovely - Ὁσα προσφιλη· Whatsoever is amiable on its own account and on account of its usefulness to others, whether in your conduct or conversation. <div eID="gen50716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50717" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever things are of good report - Ὁσα ευφημα· Whatsoever things the public agree to acknowledge as useful and profitable to men; such as charitable institutions of every kind, in which genuine Christians should ever take the lead. <div eID="gen50717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50718" type="x-p"/> If there be any virtue - If they be calculated to promote the general good of mankind, and are thus praiseworthy; <div eID="gen50718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50719" type="x-p"/> Think on these things - Esteem them highly, recommend them heartily, and practice them fervently. <div eID="gen50719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50720" type="x-p"/> Instead of ει τις επαινος, if there be any praise, several eminent MSS., as D*EFG, add επιστημης, of knowledge; and the Vulgate and the Itala have disciplinae, of discipline; but none of these appear to be an original reading.
entries.06d592d97a1a8e4eb8123cdb9de873c23f16191a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen50720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50721" type="x-p"/> Those things, which ye have - learned - From my preaching and writing; <div eID="gen50721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50722" type="x-p"/> And received - By faith, as a revelation from God; <div eID="gen50722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50723" type="x-p"/> And heard - From my preaching, and that of those who labored with me; and heard from me, in my private communications with you; and heard of me from other Churches; <div eID="gen50723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50724" type="x-p"/> And seen in me - While living and labouring among you; <div eID="gen50724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50725" type="x-p"/> Do - Take them for the rule of your faith and practice. <div eID="gen50725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50726" type="x-p"/> And the God of peace - He who is the author of peace, the lover of peace, and the maintainer of peace; he who has made peace between heaven and earth, by the mission and sacrifice of his Son, shall be ever with you while you believe and act as here recommended.
entries.850ec21e5060dca8019834c52be2bf0a7f44bdee: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen50726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50727" type="x-p"/> But I rejoiced in the Lord - Every good comes from God, either immediately from his providence or from his grace; therefore the apostle thanks God for the kindness of the Philippians towards him; for it was God that gave them the power, and directed their hearts to use it. <div eID="gen50727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50728" type="x-p"/> Hath flourished again - They had helped him before, <reference osisRef="Phi.2.25">Phi 2:25</reference>; they had ceased for a time, and now they began again. This is evidently designed by the apostle, as the word ανεθαλετε implies, which is a metaphor taken from the reviviscence of flowers in spring which seemed dead in winter. For the time in which they were apparently remiss he makes a delicate apology: Ye were careful, but ye lacked opportunity; or rather ηκαιρεισθε, ye had not ability, ye wanted the means; as the word sometimes implies.
entries.dedfe18ace803d8f8641b9212a88057188822209: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen50728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50729" type="x-p"/> Not that I speak in respect of want - I am quite unconcerned in this respect; leaving the whole of my support, while bound for the testimony of Jesus, to the providence of God. <div eID="gen50729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50730" type="x-p"/> For I have learned - I am so satisfied with the wise providence and goodness of God, that I know whatever he determines is the best; and therefore I am perfectly contented that he should govern the world in that way which seems best to his godly wisdom. How true is the proverb, A contented mind is a continual feast! What do we get by murmuring and complaining?
